title: Why M&S director Kathryn Turner is the ultimate ‘Gay Halloween’ costume idea
author: Lauren Cochrane
text:
Product development boss at Marks & Spencer inspires niche outfits after unexpected success on social media

S he is not the most likely viral star. But with 310,000 followers on TikTok and 270,000 on Instagram, Marks & Spencer Food’s director of product development, Kathryn Turner, has suddenly become one of the year’s big hits on social media. Her videos take the viewer with her as she goes in-store to look at new dessert launches, including its banana, caramel and pecan pudding, or taste test its latest products, such as its cherry and chocolate cookies .

Turner is part of Marks & Spencer’s wider social media strategy implemented in 2020 as a way of attracting younger shoppers. Instead of using traditional influencers, M&S now champions 100 of its own employees on TikTok .

Turner, who launched her account in May, now regularly receives more than 1m likes on her videos, with celebrities including Nigella Lawson and Stormzy among her followers. Part of the appeal is Turner’s insider knowledge and expertise: she has worked at M&S since 1995.

This weekend, she will gain another prestigious accolade as fans spurn ghosts, witches and vampires and instead dress up as her for Halloween . The formula is simple. Some Turner-esque glasses, a blond wig and a packet of M&S cookies.

The content creator Liam Gleed has been posting videos of himself as Turner in the run-up to Halloween and plans to wear the costume this weekend. “To be very real, I love a sweet treat and I work close to an M&S so I follow her socials to find out what snacks I’ll be getting every Friday at work,” he says. “The more niche you go for Halloween, the better. Why go as basic characters when you can dress as your current fixation or icons of the internet?”

Gleed says it is the “real person” element that appeals to him. “I think it’s quite hilarious that someone who works as a product developer at M&S can become this on social media,” he says. “That’s what made the content work so well – it is so random that she is this popular figure from quite a normal job.”

Dressing like someone such as Turner – an improbable online star – rather than a spooky character or a movie star fits into the idea of Gay Halloween. This is a way of approaching the dress-up holiday that utilises an online pop culture reference – the more specific the better. It taps into “if you know, you know” culture.

This year, that could be anything from an iced coffee at a job interview, based on a viral story about whether or not it is acceptable, to Chappell Roan’s security guard, who allegedly made a fan cry , or the prenup papers for Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s marriage.

According to the website Know Your Meme , the term Gay Halloween dates to 2023 but had a precursor in “jokes about ‘Gay Halloween’ costumes being absurdly niche” on X. The idea has now spread to everyone online, however.

“I don’t think that gay people are exclusively culpable for this,” says James Greig, features editor of Dazed. “I can remember around 2016 finding it really annoying when straight guys were going [to Halloween parties] as very, very niche memes.”

It is well documented that Halloween has been embraced by queer people owing to the holiday providing the freedom to dress up without judgment – it is sometimes called “gay Christmas” – and Gleed argues that its origins remain here.

“Personally, as a gay man, I think it’s just another way for us to express ourselves,” he says. “We aren’t afraid to be our authentic selves after coming out, and to dress as someone so niche makes it comedic gold. I think the gays are doing it best because we don’t feel that shame of getting judged because we have been anyway.”

As for which Gay Halloween costumes may be popular this year, José Criales-Unzueta, style correspondent at Vanity Fair, wrote about the trend recently. They have a few predictions beyond Turner, including references to Heated Rivalry and Drake’s recent viral poncho.

The internet is also championing a New York pothole filled by the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani , and the foliage during Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl performance . “But the best ones are the ones you cannot foresee,” says Criales-Unzueta. “Part of the magic of Gay Halloween is the unexpected.”

title: This budget fails to live up to Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric | Letters
author: Guardian Staff
text:
Caitlin Boswell of Tax Justice UK and others on what Aditya Chakrabortty described as a ‘Martin Lewis budget’

Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget ( Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October ). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham.

As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it.

So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched. Recouping the massive wealth and profits siphoned off to shady tax havens each year, equalising how the tax system treats income from wealth and work, and building HMRC’s capacity to properly measure and collect tax from the very richest would raise tens of billions to help pay for targeted, meaningful cost of living support and Burnham’s ambitious plans to fix the housing crisis, fund social care and devolve power and wealth to every region.

Reforming capital gains tax – a proposal supported by members of his own party – would make things fairer and raise around £19.7bn a year, enough to build 90,000 new council homes (the number needed each year to end the housing crisis) and train 128,000 new NHS nurses .

This government cannot survive much longer on vibes alone, and Labour is already on its last chance. Burnham must use his 10-year plan and spending review to lay out a proper roadmap to genuinely improve lives and transform the country, otherwise he risks being remembered for gherkins, which isn’t much better than Liz Truss’s lettuce. Caitlin Boswell Deputy director, external affairs, Tax Justice UK

Aditya Chakrabortty is right to say that Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric and romantic notions need to be translated into a bold programme of change. Unless this government tackles income and wealth inequality seriously, people’s anger will unceremoniously sweep it from office at the next election. Hugh Firth Newcastle upon Tyne

Living in a rented band B property, my “breathing space” was short-lived on budget day. The £100 energy payment announced by the chancellor will be entirely swallowed up by Northern Energy’s own announcement via email at 5pm the same day: “a temporary fuel surcharge of £17 per delivery will be applied to LPG deliveries as from your next delivery”.

Although this is “temporary”, customers are warned that the need to cover the elevated fuel costs is likely to remain for the foreseeable future. I had six deliveries of LPG last year – do the maths. Juliet Lunn Cockermouth, Cumbria

Once again, tax thresholds are frozen. What a missed opportunity. It would have been so easy to raise the threshold in line with the state pension, and keep them aligned. This simple mechanism would ensure that those with no other income pay no tax, and keep a little more money in the pockets of working people and others on very low incomes. Maybe next year? Jack Kenward South Molton, North Devon

Although abolishing the standing charge is something I agree with, presumably one of the groups that will benefit are second (and third) home owners. This includes approximately 177 MPs , Airbnb properties and holiday lets. John Victor Davies Hastings, East Sussex

I know that things are tight, but could the government not have funded a red box with “CR III” painted on it rather than the “ER II” sported by Mr Healey? Robert Bowden Bristol

title: Review: The Exposure Strada 13 RS Light Begs You to Ride a Little Longer
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Headlights for road riding need to do different things for different people. For some, it’s just about the bare minimum: something for cars to see and to illuminate the road so drivers can spot upcoming potholes. For others, it is a key tool in their stable: big lights that power early or late rides that salvage exercise in the hectic pace of a busy life.

For most of my life, I have been the former. My headlights have been just enough to be seen in the dawn and dusk. As I have gotten older, however, that has changed. Lights have become more important as my time to ride has shifted to the early morning hours that are the bread and butter of Phoenix, Arizona, riding.

Lights are now essential kit that I have to think about differently. It is technology I need more from.

Exposure Lights has built a brand upon that attitude. The small UK-based shop has grown to prominence with lights that match reliable performance, long battery life, and sleek aesthetics.

Nowhere has this been more obvious than with the brand’s new Strada 13 RS light. As I have ventured deeper into the night as the seasons have changed, the Strada has been a fantastic companion in getting much more out of night riding.

Despite a size that is typically reserved for off-road-focused lights, the Strada 13 is a purpose-built tool for road riding. Chief among those features is the lights’ auto-dimming AKTiv technology.

AKTiv is automatically configured on the Strada 13 and is set to dim its beam when it senses an oncoming car. The AKTiv technology has been a fixture on previous models, but the new Strada has two sensors that allow for increased precision. On rides, this makes for rapid adjustments that keep my hands on the bars and the driver from being blasted by a few hundred lumens of light.

Speaking of lumens, while it might seem that the bigger light is there for more lumens, that isn’t exactly the case. Exposure does pack more lumens in smaller packages, like the Diablo off-road light. The size of the light is more for the battery life and the added road-based functionality.

That battery has been a huge plus in my riding. While I haven’t yet ridden through the night with it yet—which would certainly be possible for the Strada 13 on one charge—the longevity of the battery has been a huge benefit.

Compared to smaller lights, I have been thrilled by the combination of a powerful beam and the set-it-and-forget-it battery life. Through a full week of riding, with more than a few hours before dark, the light can stay on with no issues.

To put it plainly, 217g is a lot of weight for a light. Part of me loves a small, easy-to-add headlight for road riding. The Exposure’s Sirius 11 road light is a mere 90g, and it can still kick up to 1,300 lumens. Yet, it doesn’t have the same adjustability, beam range, and most significantly, battery life.

Previously, if I had the choice of a light the size of the Sirius and the Strada for the fast group ride, I would have picked the Sirius every time. Now, the choice is not so clear-cut, although if I were measuring my night riding time in minutes and not hours, I would still perhaps pick the Sirius for its weight and sleek size.

The other real wonky aspect of the light is the single-button interface. It takes a bit of trial and error to figure out how the sequencing of button presses yields the desired results. Even so, I find that I don’t always get the light to do what I want straightaway. There is a way to bring some of the light controls and displays to any head unit to make that functionality simpler. But, straight out of the box, it is less than intuitive.

The Strada is perhaps most useful as a piece of kit that is low maintenance, easy to use, and easy to swap between bikes if you have multiple mounts.

The light has two attachments, one for a 31.9-diameter round bar and the other for an action mount that can be attached to an integrated computer mount, and both are stripped down but sturdy. Both mounts put the light further forward, away from the bike to provide a better position to illuminate the periphery of the road. That said, with the added weight, be sure to check the weight tolerances of the mounts before using the light since it could push the weight limit in some cases.

All of my riding with the light thus far has been with the action mount attached to the bar mount for the Trek Domane I have been testing with. It has been incredibly easy to use, easy to set up, and the big light almost disappears underneath the computer mount and bar. Out of sight, out of mind rings very true for a big headlight.

Lastly, with a USB-C cable port, the light is always easy to find a charger for. It can also be easily flipped and used to top up other electronics in a pinch. While the battery might last a while, charging it takes much less time. With the optimal cable, the Strada will fully charge in two hours.

The Exposure Strada 13 RS is for two types of riders: those who ride at night multiple times a week, and those who will measure their time riding in the dark in hours rather than minutes. If you fit those categories, this is one of the best tech adds you can make to boost the quality of your rides. It is good enough to be that transformative.

To learn more, check out Exposure Light’s website , and to see more bike lights, visit our best bike lights buyer’s guide .

title: Indoor cycling is boring, discuss – A for-and-against debate on the sport's most polarising training tool
author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
text:
It’s Indoor Cycling Week here at , a week in which we centre our tech content on the fast-growing world of virtual cycling.

We’re all different, so this article is going to explore the other side of the virtual coin.

Even here within the editorial team, there’s a broad range of opinion. I personally rather enjoy cycling indoors. It’s convenient, structured, safe, and I can know what time I’ll be finished with to-the-minute precision, making planning it into my day perfectly easy.

But others here hate it. On one recent call, one of my colleagues’ immediate replies was: “I’d rather pull my nails out.”

That, and other things mentioned below, are a few of the opinions that have been flying around amongst the CN Team this week, so we thought we would package them up for you to enjoy. They might ruffle some feathers, but balance and honesty are important in journalism, so hopefully we don’t upset too many people.

Indoor training doesn't make a peloton-ready cyclist

When I was racing, I had a love-hate relationship with my indoor trainers. This was before Zwift and the gamification of cycling, when riders only spent time on the trainer if they had broken an arm, had to work during the short daylight hours, or it was snowing. When I had to ride indoors, it was usually one focussed hour of intervals.

Maybe it's because I was a competitive swimmer as a kid and was used to counting minutes of effort and seconds of rest without outside entertainment - but some loud music or an old Paris-Roubaix replay on the TV for inspiration was more than enough.

I miss the days when indoor training was a much-loathed necessity

I've done my time on Zwift, and the gamification aspect can inspire riders to make impressive aerobic fitness and strength gains. However, for me, it de-emphasises what is the best part of being a cyclist is: being immersed in the flow of the peloton, learning etiquette from the more experienced riders, getting fit together and then pushing faster and further than you could ever do on your own.

I remember doing a 'century' (100 miles/161km) in the flatter part of eastern North Carolina with a well-disciplined group of about 20 riders, just pace-lining, no attacks or other hijinks, and finishing in four hours. No stops, no rest, just beautifully efficient at 40kph.

But then came the apps, and dudes started showing up at group rides with impressive fitness from a winter of Zwift, with all the confidence of a member of the masochist club, absolutely no idea how to ride in a group, and zero interest in learning. They were an absolute menace in the bunch: hostile to any advice, frustratingly resistant to being flicked out the back, disrupting the flow completely with attacks, and totally ruining the vibe.

Yes, I'm a curmudgeon, but I really miss the days when indoor training was a much-loathed necessity and road cycling was an in-person collective effort, not just a chance to show off your watts/kg on the no-drop group ride. I think the beauty of a peloton moving like a murmuration at speed is an essential part of cycling culture - and one that an app just cannot teach.

'I don’t hate it as much as I used to'

Let’s get this straight: indoor cycling is not my happy place, but on the other hand, I don’t hate as much as I used to. For me, cycling is about being outside; it might be a cliché, but I enjoy the wind in my face, experiencing the day whether it’s warm or cold, feeling the tyres rolling; it’s all so much better than staring at a closed garage door. It’s a bit sad that someone my age sees every ride as an adventure, but I do; when I ride, I’ve been somewhere and done something.

It’s also about joy. But joy is not clattering into potholes in the dark, and riding in the rain is one of the least joyful things I’ve ever done voluntarily. I won’t ride in the rain; I own a rain jacket, but I’ve only worn it three times in six years. This is where the turbo trainer comes in.

I’m not going to race again, and I can’t remember the last time I did an organised event, so I’m not ‘training’, but I want to continue enjoying outdoor rides and maintain my overall fitness; a bit of exertion stops me getting grumpy, too. So when the days are short, or the weather is bad, you will find me on the turbo.

Back when ‘dumb’ trainers were the only option, I hated it and set a limit of 30 minutes, but a smart turbo and indoor apps make it doable, and much better. Picking one of the workouts on Zwift helps me add some structure, and more importantly, some interest to my indoor riding. It’s also time-efficient; I get a decent workout from an indoor ride, and sometimes it’s even fun as well as productive.

But for me it’s a solo affair. Maybe it’d be better with all the groups, chats and messages, but I’m not interested, partly because I’m a little antisocial and partly because I don’t wear my glasses as they steam up. I won’t notice if you’ve given me one of those thumbs-up Ride On things because unless it’s a very easy session, I just can’t see.

Indoor cycling isn’t going to make me a better bike handler; I won’t have any meaningful social interaction, and it can’t replicate the richness that riding outside creates in my soul. But it does help my fitness and provides a close enough facsimile of the real thing that I get genuine satisfaction out of it. I am now off to ride Zwift for a while; I just won’t see you if you’re there.

Give me a training plan, an erg mode workout and make me follow a line on a graph and I can pluck up the motivation, so long as I know there’s an end goal being pursued. Put me in a virtual world and ask me to ‘free ride’, and I’ll be bored in 10 minutes. I know it’s basically the same principle as ‘free riding’ outside, but the flow state I experience with steering, wind and tyre noise, cars passing, route planning and so on, just doesn’t come when it’s a virtual avatar pedalling awkwardly through a pixelated landscape. Even with the advent of in-game steering and the noise of the fan, I get bored.

Invariably I open YouTube or Netflix, or I get off the bike.

That’s not to say indoor cycling is bad. It can definitely serve a purpose, and to have helped more people be more active, I’m all for it. But it’s not fun. Not the type 1 variety anyway.

I love riding bikes outside, but I also used to get a perverse satisfaction from my old school, wheel-on trainer in combination with a stopwatch, a towel, and somewhere to be sick. It got me very fit for racing cyclo-cross, and while it didn't replicate the fun of riding outside it was efficient, and masochistic in a way that pottering about up a pretend volcano can never replicate.

The thing I love about outdoor cycling is the effort in combination with all of the lovely sensations, but in the absence of those lovely sensations of cornering, wind, a snotty nose, the spray of leaf mulch on my shins, and the abominable noise of modern freehubs, I just want .

Modern indoor training isn't rubbish because it doesn't replicate outdoors well enough, it's rubbish because it puts too many barriers between me and getting my heart rate up to something approaching maximum while I listen to Bullet For My Valentine. I don't want to log into an app , realise the WiFi connection is spotty, dig out the extender, pair my trainer and heart rate monitor with the laptop, update nine different firmwares, choose a course, realise that bit of the map is locked, choose a different course, wait for it to buffer.... and finally ride. At each of those steps the risk of me just giving up in frustration becomes higher.

I just want a machine to provide resistance and a brick wall to stare at. I don't want to race a man from Finland. I know it's still possible, but it's becoming much rarer.

The contrasting (positive) opinion: Indoor offers almost everything I need from cycling

For me, cycling is not about the wind in my hair, an in-the-moment adventure or finding the path less travelled. It’s about being competitive, racing, testing myself and sprinting for the finish line with a chance of victory.

Riding outdoors teaches a part of that: bunch etiquette, handling, tyre grip limits and so on. But once you’ve got those skills, they don’t need much refinement. And without a good foundation of fitness, those skills aren’t particularly useful anyway.

And riding outdoors is fine for building that foundation of fitness, but I can do it much more quickly and comprehensively on a smart trainer with a machine forcing me to ride at a set power output. It also means an hour of riding takes about an hour and five minutes. Unlike riding outside in winter, where an hour’s ride takes close to two hours, once you factor in getting changed twice and cleaning the bike.

A few years ago, I spent an entire summer training indoors for the British Gravel National Championships. Knowing the route wasn’t technical, and knowing I had bunch etiquette down from years of racing on the road, I don’t think I did more than four or five rides outside before the race. I finished fourth.

title: Who Really Deserves the Vélo d’Or? Let the Debate Begin
author: ahood
text:
Who's the best rider in cycling? The Velo d'Or prize tries to answer that. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Who is the best rider in pro cycling? The Velo d’Or prize tries to answer that.

The road season is over, but there’s still some prizes to dole out with cycling’s most prestigious and sometimes controversial awards.

L’Équipe revealed the nominees Thursday, with the winners set to collect their trophies November 28 at the Fairmont Monte Carlo in Monaco in a posh, Oscar night-style party.

Some of these are no-brainers. Demi Vollering will be the overwhelming favorite after winning a second yellow jersey and her first rainbow title.

Tadej Pogačar could match Alberto Contador as the all-time winner of four times. He’ll face off against the likes of world champion Brandon McNulty, French phenom Paul Seixas, and Vuelta winner Enric Mas.

There’s more hardware up for grabs this year, too. Four new awards will honor the best male and female sprinters and rookies, with fans deciding the rookie winners.

Created by Vélo Magazine in 1992, the Vélo d’Or – the “golden bike” in French — is cycling’s answer to soccer’s Ballon d’Or.

Winners are chosen by an international panel of cycling journalists based on wins, star power, versatility, and panache . (Full disclosure: I’m on that jury. And whittling down the winners can be harder than you’d think.)

But will Pogačar’s injury-shortened season undercut his chances of winning? Let’s dive in.

This one should be a sure bet. Vollering dominated every race she started, and won her second yellow jersey and her first world title.

Lorena Wiebes could pick up some votes for her dominance in the sprints, but she’ll be a lock for that new award. Spain’s Paula Blasi — who recently penned a blockbuster deal with Movistar — could be an outsider.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney — winner on Mont Ventoux — and Marlen Reusser are other contenders, but this one’s all but certain for DemVol .

A stand-alone women’s category was created in 2022, and Vollering could become the first repeat winner.

The big name missing? Defending winner Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, although she’s still in the running for the French women’s award.

Even with crashing out of the Vuelta a España and missing the worlds, Pogačar will probably win again, but his stiffest competition could come from within his UAE Emirates-XRG team bus.

Isaac del Toro and newly crowned world champion McNulty — the only American nominated — join him on the shortlist, giving UAE three of the 10 spots.

How to measure up Pogačar’s season? King Pog absolutely dominated the 2026 season, and only a superb Wout van Aert could deny him Paris-Roubaix. A crash doesn’t diminish his fantastic season, but his absence did open the doors for many on this list.

Mas brings a Vuelta title, while Seixas gets a seat alongside some of the biggest names of the past decade. Remco Evenepoel was unstoppable against the clock, McNulty won America’s first rainbow since the 1990s, and Van Aert could be an emotional favorite.

The classics awards give the one-day specialists their own moment on the stage, although there’s plenty of crossover with the main event.

This sometimes can get sloppy. With today’s top riders so versatile, it’s hard to pigeon-hole a rider like Pogačar into one category.

A few years ago, fans were outraged when Mathieu van der Poel was named best classics rider and Pogačar won the overall prize. Can that happen again this year?

All five men’s finalists also made the overall shortlist. On the women’s side, Lotte Kopecky and Puck Pieterse are hoping to win based on what they delivered on a single afternoon.

Women : Franziska Koch, Lotte Kopecky, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Puck Pieterse and Demi Vollering.

Men : Remco Evenepoel, Tadej Pogačar, Paul Seixas, Wout van Aert and Mathieu van der Poel.

The fast finishers finally see their own trophies this year. About time, some might say.

The new awards give sprinting its due, especially with sprinters increasingly seeing fewer opportunities to shine as grand tours have become more challenging over the past two decades (though the men’s 2027 Tour de France sees a revival of sorts).

Wiebes is the only rider on both the women’s sprint and overall shortlists. Matthew Brennan has two chances here, with nominations for sprinting and the rookie prize.

Women : Elisa Balsamo, Lara Gillespie, Charlotte Kool, Nienke Veenhoven and Lorena Wiebes.

Men : Matthew Brennan, Paul Magnier, Tim Merlier, Jonathan Milan and Jasper Philipsen.

Want an actual vote? The new rookie awards are where fans get their say .

And “rookie” comes with some fine print. Riders qualify through standout performances on their first appearance at a grand tour, monument, or world championships, so they don’t necessarily have to be first-year pros.

Paula Blasi and Seixas are also nominated for the main awards.

Women : Paula Blasi, Célia Gery and Isabella Holmgren.

Men : Matthew Brennan, Jakob Omrzel and Paul Seixas.

The French rider awards means the hometown stars won’t leave empty-handed, with Seixas appearing on his fourth shortlist of the evening.

Women : Juliette Berthet, Marion Bunel, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, Célia Gery and Cédrine Kerbaol.

Men : Dorian Godon, Romain Grégoire, Paul Magnier, Lenny Martinez and Paul Seixas.

For the main Vélo d’Or awards, each journalist ranks five riders from the respective 10-person lists. First gets five points, second gets four, and so on down to one point for fifth.

Sounds straightforward until you’re staring at the ballot and trying to decide who gets left off.

The ceremony will hand out 12 awards, including para-cycling honors, and will air live on L’Équipe ’s free-to-air French television channel.

I’ve got some decisions to make. Who’s in your top five?

title: Thousands of “ghost students” use AI to steal millions in student loans, DOJ says
author: Ashley Belanger
text:
The US has charged five individuals as part of the first broad federal crackdown on “ghost students”—fraudsters who steal the identities of hundreds of Americans to pose as fake college students and steal student loans.

In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from “a network associated with Kenyan nationals" after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that “this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya,” while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun.

“If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build a future—we will find you,” McDonald said. “Whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you.”

title: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’
author: Dan Milmo and Kalyeena Makortoff
text:
Binance said the extent of damages was not known and had not confirmed whether funds had been pilfered

Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it is investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”.

It wasn’t immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to accomplish and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered, but stablecoin issuers quickly froze funds Thursday evening.

“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement continued.

Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.

Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen more than an equivalent of $800m in currency associated with the incident “in coordination with law enforcement”. Paolo Ardoino, the CEO of Tether, said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5bn in currency related to “a potential Binance exchange hack”.

The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday afternoon to under $79,000.

title: Hamilton on why he is “built differently” to stay in F1 for the “foreseeable future”
What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?
text:
When Sir Jim Ratcliffe became a co-owner of Manchester United in 2024, much of the narrative centred on his desire to rebuild the club around a British core.

Given the expense of buying homegrown players, and the difficulties Michael Carrick - the first permanent British managerial appointment of the Ineos era - has faced this season, perhaps Ratcliffe is rethinking.

But if Carrick fails to stop the rot and loses his job, United are already considering the merits of appointing another British coach - albeit one who is more experienced.

That Eddie Howe is a contender for a job that remains one of the most high-profile in world football isn't hard to fathom.

Speak to those who have worked alongside Howe and they describe a man whose track record of improving players is a direct result of his relentless approach on the training field.

They will also tell you Howe is someone who places an unwavering importance on the methodology of setting a winning culture.

Howe may lack experience at one of the traditional top-six clubs, but his body of work at Bournemouth and Newcastle is impressive.

Having been appointed Bournemouth boss with the club facing relegation from League Two in January 2009, Howe led them to the Premier League in 2015. He went on to establish the Cherries as a top-flight club before leaving - for a second time - in 2020.

In 2021, Howe was appointed Newcastle manager. He led them from relegation trouble to qualification for the Champions League on two occasions and won the EFL Cup - the club's first trophy in 56 years - in 2025.

Man Utd stick with Carrick - inside a turbulent 48 hours at Old Trafford

Of course, managing Manchester United is an altogether different proposition.

Indeed, Howe's emergence as a potential successor to Carrick has been greeted with negativity in some circles.

Sections of the fanbase have been vocal on social media with their opinion that Howe isn't a big enough name to replace Carrick.

Former United players Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt also fell short of providing their backing to Howe on their podcast, though it is worth pointing out they spoke in favour of the 48-year-old's potential appointment when Ruben Amorim was sacked in January.

Ex-captain Roy Keane is among those to have backed Howe as a possible successor to Carrick, and other former top-flight players - including Darren Bent, Gareth Barry and Jack Wilshere - have also touted him as the man for the job.

Of course, if you look hard enough you'll find voices for and against every potential manager, and it will be up to United chief executive Omar Berrada, sporting director Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell to weigh up how they proceed.

Their first decision will be what happens with Carrick, and Saturday's match against Chelsea is likely to have a bearing on how United move forward.

If Carrick does depart, finances will inevitably be a factor.

The former Middlesbrough boss and his staff will need to be paid up before United even get to factoring in the monetary commitment towards their next head coach.

While the details of Howe's agreement with Newcastle when he left in the summer remain confidential, it is understood that as things stand any club or national team would be required to pay a seven-figure compensation fee to the Magpies.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle - with a view to protecting themselves against Howe walking straight into another club - reached an agreement over a compensation structure that decreases over time.

It is understood that figure started at £6m but has already reduced by half.

The compensation payments have an expiry date - understood to be before the end of the season - at which point he can be appointed for nothing.

Of course, in an industry in which astronomical figures are the norm, the prospect of paying a maximum of £3m for Howe may not be too problematic.

That said, given the amount Manchester United have spent on hiring and firing managers in recent years, it is understandable if Berrada and Wilcox want to keep costs down.

How talking about Man Utd's cycle of doom became an industry

As well as the doubts from some supporters about Howe's potential appointment, there has also been conjecture over how he would fit in United's footballing structure.

At both Bournemouth and Newcastle, Howe developed a strong powerbase in all aspects of the footballing department - including recruitment.

That dynamic wasn't without financial benefit to Howe's employers.

The likes of Nathan Ake, Callum Wilson and Tyrone Mings were all signed by Howe at Bournemouth - and sold for a big profit by the Cherries.

At Newcastle, meanwhile, Howe was instrumental in the signings of Bruno Guimarares, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Alexander Isak - all of whom were sold for more than they joined for. Dan Burn, Lewis Hall and Tino Livramento are among those to have developed into full England internationals under his coaching.

But with a football management structure at Old Trafford that includes Berrada, Wilcox and Vivell, it is likely that Howe - at least not immediately - would not be afforded the same level of autonomy.

Howe, though, is on record saying he is happy to work alongside sporting directors, and has a track record of doing so - firstly at Bournemouth under Richard Hughes, then chief executive Neill Blake.

At Newcastle, he worked closely with senior management figures Dan Ashworth, Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi - so fitting into Manchester United's structure wouldn't be drastically different.

Whether he would want the job given the challenges, we may never know. And ultimately it is the opinion of Manchester United's decision-makers that will truly matter.

Howe is an obvious contender for the Manchester United job, just as he would be if the England head coach's position became available.

Whether he is offered it or not will give a clear indication about the path United are going down.…

title: Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed
author: Sarah Butler
text:
With the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conduct

‘I t was a very successful and simple proposition,” laments one former Poundland boss. With every product in the shop sold at £1, and the price in its name, its proposition to shoppers was the clearest of any UK high street chain.

Now the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer could disappear amid heavy competition and inflation that has eaten into its ability to offer bargains.

Its potential collapse has brought distress for its up to 12,000 staff in the run-up to Christmas, and as shoppers head to the chain for Halloween costumes and treats.

Meanwhile, its low-profile owners are facing questions from the prime minister over their behaviour in the week his government’s budget attempted to offer support to the high street .

Poundland’s future hangs in the balance – and not for the first time – after the 36-year-old retailer filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.

The legal measure protects Poundland, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland, from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the prospect of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers hold back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.

The chain’s potential demise comes after Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring specialist which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner in June last year, rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the whole chain by Martin Property Group.

While the Northern Irish firm is still in talks about taking on Poundland, it is understood its offer amounts to about £15m. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood.

This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, Poundland’s former owner, which holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News.

One source who knows Poundland well said that Gordon Brothers had already taken about £10m in fees and interest out of the chain in the last year and that wanting another £30m was “egregious”. Gordon Brothers did not respond to a request for comment and has not confirmed this figure.

Gordon Brothers said earlier this week that options for the whole and parts of the business “are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland’s people and all relevant stakeholders”.

Sources close to the process said Gordon Brothers was unwilling to accept the Martin deal as the latest offer includes only about £7.5m up front and the rest over the next two years, leaving uncertainty for creditors, staff and suppliers.

One source said Gordon Brothers had sought bidders for the whole of Poundland but “the market had spoken” and only one little-known financial bidder with no history of running a large retail chain in the UK had come forward who might only go on to break up Poundland itself.

Instead, the restructuring specialist is understood to believe that suppliers and staff would be safer with the “trusted established retail operators” who have already put forward firm offers for parcels of outlets that amount to about half of Poundland’s stores, which could be converted to their formats.

A deal may yet be agreed with Martin over the next 10 days, especially with political pressure from Andy Burnham. On Friday, he told the Telegraph: “We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.”

For now, Gordon Brothers appears more keen on a break-up after losing faith in the likelihood of Poundland finding a route to long-term profitability amid tough times on the high street and heavy competition.

Rapid inflation on the cost of goods and labour, energy and business rates in recent years has forced Poundland to take a hit on profits and sell products for more than £1, including items for £5 or more.

In the past, Poundland removed products if it could not sell them profitably for a pound, but its choices have become more limited. High inflation – triggered first by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and then the Middle East conflict – has exposed a business model which always appeared to have a shelf life.

In most supermarkets a two-litre bottle of milk costs over £2, a pack of KitKats is at least £1.50 and a tin of Heinz baked beans is about £1.40, according to the price comparison site Trolley. Cutting the size of Poundland has, meanwhile, reduced its scale, making it harder to get good deals from suppliers to protect margins.

Poundland has also admitted that it made mistakes in recent years, including putting its Pepco clothing ranges into stores, which proved unpopular with UK shoppers.

The expansion of cut-price chains such as Savers, The Range, B&M, The Works and Home Bargains alongside budget online rivals such as Temu, Shein and Amazon means the cheaper end of the UK retail market is now very crowded.

Meanwhile, the low-wage shoppers that make up the core of Poundland’s clientele have little spare cash for non-essentials amid rising household bills . Those with more to spare have more options in their supermarket shop, where they are increasingly locked in by loyalty-card-linked discounts.…

title: Analysts find looming launch crisis is "more severe" than anticipated
author: Eric Berger
text:
A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years.

The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.

"What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. "What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s."

title: Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
text:
Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency.

Nicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.

In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was the "right time" to leave her post.

Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for taking £1.9m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2026, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance.

The payments were made by Yorkshire Water's parent company, Kelda Holdings, for what the firm said was "investor engagement" and "financial oversight".

On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company".

The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011.

In 2024, Ofwat announced it was fining the company £47m for historic sewage leaks .

In her statement, Shaw said: "It has been a privilege to lead Yorkshire Water and serve the people of Yorkshire.

"Although there remains a huge amount of work to do, I am extremely proud of what our colleagues have achieved, putting the business on a stronger footing for delivery across all aspects of its work."

Yorkshire Water said Medalova would join the company on Monday as part of a transition period before assuming the chief executive officer role full time in the new year.

She said: "I am delighted to be joining Yorkshire Water and grateful to the board for the opportunity to lead the business through its next chapter.

"Yorkshire Water faces huge challenges but also great opportunities for continued improvement and I look forward to working with Nicola Shaw, the leadership team and colleagues across the business as I get up to speed."

In December last year Shaw said "not being transparent" about receiving £1.3m in shareholder-funded payments across two instalments had been a "mistake" , but had insisted those amounts were "not for me to decide".

She received a further £660,000 earlier this year. Ofwat said the payments were not performance-related.

The previously undisclosed payments had come to light the previous August when the government banned Yorkshire Water and five other water companies from paying "unfair" bonuses to bosses .

Tom Gordon, Liberal Democrat MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, said Shaw should have stepped down "much earlier".

"Good riddance. Nicola Shaw oversaw abysmal management of our precious natural resources, trashing our rivers while receiving an eye-watering salary," he said.

"Her replacement needs to understand that residents are at their wits' end, paying ever-rising bills for polluted rivers and threats of hosepipe bans while someone at the top rakes in millions."

Meanwhile, Judith Cummins, Labour MP for Bradford South, said Yorkshire Water needed "more than a change of leadership" but a "complete change of direction".

"A new face at the top cannot wash away years of Yorkshire Water failing to put customers first," she said.

"Nicola Shaw's time as Yorkshire Water boss saw customers frustrated by poor service, skyrocketing bills, record pollution incidents, and a plummet from 'good' to the worst possible one-star environment rating.

"There must be a wholesale shift in culture that finally prioritises customers. Only then can the company begin to restore public trust."

title: USPro criterium star Luke Elphingstone, 'a Michael Matthews kind of rider', among three national champions featured in younger Project Echelon Racing squad for 2027
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Three national champions feature on a leaner roster for Project Echelon Racing in 2027. The team are adding five new riders to a lineup with eight returning teammates, three of those having performed as stagiaires last season.

The trimmed roster of 13 riders moves the average age from 25.5 to 22.6 years, in what the team called a "big transition year", their fifth at the UCI Continental level. Seven familiar faces depart, including Eric Brunner , Ricky Arnopol, Stephen Bassett , and Laurent Gervais, who have been with the team for the past three or more years.

"These guys have been with me for a long time and helped me build a really strong legacy with Project Echelon. Retiring or just moving on, the majority of the guys were going to be leaving, and I wanted to give them an opportunity to leave on their own terms and move on to a different phase of life," Eric Hill, Project Echelon Racing team director and non-profit co-founder, told

Arnopol and Gervais are retiring, while others were "just taking a different direction", such as Bassett, a former USPro criterium champion, and Brunner, a three-time US elite cyclo-cross champion who was expected to begin his 'cross season at Cycle-Smart Northampton Cyclocross UCI C2 races in Massachusetts. Caleb Classen, Quinn Felton and Ethan Craine also bid farewell.

Hill was excited to have consistency with "cornerstone" riders back, such as Tim McBirney, who was third overall at the 2026 Tour de Beauce, as well as versatility with Brendan Rhim and Colby Lange, who have been with the team for four and five years, respectively. Second-year riders Elphingstone and Gauthier will showcase their national jerseys with the team's international calendar.

"He's a Michael Matthews kind of rider. If it's a straight-up drag race sprint, he's going to be in the mix," Hill said about the 23-year-old Elphingstone, who performed well in stage races with stage wins at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and Tour de Bloom, then a podium at the Tour of Samsun in Turkey in the back half of last season.

"Jérôme's just an absolute grinder, and you know, when things are uncomfortable, and people want to start giving up is kind of when he shines," Hill added about the 22-year-old Canadian.

Gauthier finished second at the UCI 1.2 Gran Premio New York City and scored 4 top 10s at Tour de Beauce, including a podium on the final day in Saint-Georges, to win the youth classification. However, it was at Canadian road nationals, where he won the elite road race and, with it, also secured the U23 title, that exhibited that true grit.

"It was cold and raining and windy and miserable, to the point where they had to take down the finish banners because it was too windy and postpone the podium celebration. He just thrives in that type of gritty environment, and he made it happen for himself."

A trio of stagiaires return to the squad on one-year contracts: 19-year-old Canadian Jacob Roy and 20-year-old US talents, Ben Boroff and Noah Shelton.

Boroff caught attention for a stage win at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and then held the points competition lead in the American Criterium Cup for several weeks until he went to Turkey to race for Project Echelon. Shelton was also on the late-season swing to Europe and impressed with a stage podium at Tour of Istanbul.

Two 19-year-olds debut Project Echelon: Canadian Arnaud Lajoie, who moves from Team Skyline and US rider Garrett Beshore, who rode with Roy and Kreikemeier at Meridian Racing.

Kreikemeier made his big step this year at USPro Road Nationals, winning the U23 ITT. He rode the last three seasons with small Spanish squads, his best season in 2024 in national stage races, sixth overall at Vuelta a Ávila and second on GC at the Vuelta Zamora.

The final two new riders are Dylan Fluckiger, 24, who has a US collegiate medal in the time trial, and Jesse Maris, 22, a native of Washington in the Pacific Northwest who had a breakout ride at the Volta a Portugal U23 stage race, placing in the top 10 in all four stages and finishing third on GC.

The team starts 2027 with a camp in Southern California at the end of January and will transition for racing and more training in Arizona with Valley of the Sun and Tucson Bicycle Classic stage races. They will travel in the spring to Croatia, Spain and Portugal for racing before a swing back for Redlands Bicycle Classic, then to Tour of Norway.

They'll have a long North American campaign through the end of June with the back half of the year in Europe. A special focus will be on three US races – the Armed Forces Cycling Classic, Battenkill, and Philadelphia Cycling Classic.

"To have this kind of resurgence of some of these one-day classics in North America, and to be able to end our season with all of these, is really important to us. Especially these guys that are retiring [and were] at Philadelphia this year, Ricky and Laurent, was really cool to see."

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘He’s a great guy to play off’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
Cup Basketball is back, and with that…

…so are your reigning Champs.

Here’s a bunch of quotes before today’s affair.

On Rick Brunson suggesting the Tyler Kolek-Jalen Brunson backcourt combination against Chicago:

“One of the things he suggested was throwing Kolek in the game with Jalen [Brunson].”

On Kolek’s performance in the Knicks’ comeback victory over the Bulls:

“Tyler had a big floor game for us.”

On Kolek’s role once Jose Alvarado return:

“Tyler is definitely going to keep playing while Jose is out. When he comes back, we’ll figure it out.”

On the need for avoiding the opening-night mistakes that doomed the Knicks:

“We just need to obviously not do what we did [the last time we played them].”

On avoiding turnovers and making smarter decisions as the Knicks’ backup point guard:

“Not trying to make the home run play. Just trying to get us in the offense, get the best shot for our team. It’s about being more mature in my game. Trying to take care of the ball, that’s what the team needs. When I go in there, I can’t be turning it over, I can’t be throwing it all over the floor. Got to get us in the offense, got to get us good shots.”

On playing alongside Jalen Brunson and benefiting from the defensive attention he attracts:

“We played together last season for stretches. He’s a great guy to play off. They’re going to double-team him, you get open shots.”

On the defensive challenges of playing in a two-point-guard lineup and staying ready for opportunities:

“Obviously it’s two smaller guards, so I have to compete harder on defense.

title: Items stolen from Man Utd Munich air disaster memorial
text:
A glass sculpture and medals have been stolen from a memorial to the 23 people killed in the Munich air disaster, including eight Manchester United players.

The items were taken from a display case at Manchesterplatz in Munich, where the plane crashed on take-off on 6 February 1958 after refuelling on its return from a European Cup match in Belgrade.

Munich Police told German media the glass was smashed with a stone and said the incident was believed to have happened between 08:00 and 13:00 local time on Monday, 26 October.

The Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF) said it was "deeply saddened", while its chair, Ifty Ahmed, said the theft had caused emotional harm to families.

"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ahmed told BBC News.

He said the memorial had provided solace for families who lost loved ones in the crash.

"And whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories," he said.

Mark Salzmann, chairman of Red Docs Munich, a Bayern Munich supporters' group which helps care for the memorial, said his mother discovered the damage while driving past.

Salzmann said a glass sculpture originally presented to Munich's former mayor, Dieter Reiter, was among the stolen items.

His group collects tributes left by visitors from around the world and places some of them in the display case.

He said the objects were unique and could not easily be replaced, but the group was discussing possible replacements with the foundation.

Ahmed said it was still unclear exactly how many medals were missing.

He said Manchester United had offered to pay for repairs, but the foundation had already agreed to cover the costs itself.

The broken glass was replaced on the same day, according to the foundation.

Ahmed said supporters of Liverpool, Manchester City and Leeds had also sent messages of support.

A memorial stone was installed in 2004, while the display case was added in 2020 and officially inaugurated in 2023.

About 1,500 people from around the world attended the annual remembrance service at Manchesterplatz in February, according to the foundation.

Salzmann said the messages of support he had received showed how important the memorial was, adding that the connection between Manchester and Munich "will never go away".

The BBC has contacted Munich Police and Manchester United for comment.

title: Pivot LES SL Drop Bar Review: Taking Gravel to the Extreme
author: Josh Ross
text:
100mm travel fork Not as heavy as you’d think 2.4” tire clearance Dropper post compatible

Low saddle to bar drop Heavy Fork bobs and requires more technique than is typical for drop bar Lacks top tube mounts Boost spacing limit wheel and crank choices Max 38t chainring

In the search for what the future of gravel bikes will look like, one obvious direction is to take the concept all the way to mountain bikes. Half the comments already claim that modern gravel bikes are just mountain bikes anyway, so why not embrace the concept? The Pivot LES SL Drop Bar belongs to exactly this class of bike. The bike is a hardtail mountain bike with drop bars.

Pivot is not unique in offering something like this, and in the past, I’ve been somewhat of a critic of the idea. It’s easy to say this kind of bike is just a parts-bin grab. A brand has a bunch of unsold mountain bike frames, so what if someone looking at the numbers just sources a cockpit that will work? Now you’ve got a whole new category of riders to potentially sell a bike to, and investment is minimal.

If you follow that line of thinking, then you also realize the result will be a compromise. The Pivot LES SL is a lightweight carbon hardtail, and it wasn’t designed for drop-bar duties. The rear end uses boost spacing, so cranks and wheels designed for gravel bikes don’t fit. Good luck finding aero-focused wheels, and the bars that are specced are massively wide compared to shoulder sizes. Now that I’ve spent time with the bike, though, is that fair? Let’s get into my revised way of looking at a bike like this.

The best thing, and the worst thing, about this bike is the 100mm front suspension. In a way, I hate it, because unlike gravel suspension that often works as a set-and-forget kind of thing, the 100mm Fox front fork requires some recalibration. If you are used to something like the RockShox Rudy front suspension, this fork might bug you because it moves a lot. If you stand to sprint, good luck. It becomes a bobbing energy suck, and you are going to want to make liberal use of the lockout and adjustment knob. You will probably also want to adopt a much more mountain-bike-style riding stance, where standing to pedal is rare and you keep your weight back.

Despite all of that, this feature is what I like about the bike because it is, in large part, the entire point. If you prefer the feel and capabilities of a 30mm or 40mm front suspension fork, then this isn’t the bike for you. If you instead need the capabilities of an actual mountain bike, then you want that full 100mm of suspension goodness, and that’s worth putting up with the compromises. It feels like you can roll over anything that comes ahead of you, and this much suspension means better traction when you do it.

This fork is also what you want if you plan to spend days or weeks traveling across seriously rough terrain. Not the kind of terrain that a short-travel gravel fork can handle, but rough, rooted, and rocky singletrack across a country. You are going to be seated while pedaling, and as you roll over things, your hands and arms don’t have to be in a constant state of tension.

Now that I, as the resident roadie in our gravel bike Field Test, got to spend time with a bike in this category, I could also make the argument that this is what you want as a road-leaning rider. If you feel unsure of yourself when things get truly rough, then big suspension (for a drop-bar bike) is what will make the difference between always feeling unsure and really starting to feel capable. Just make sure you don’t expect to do too much mixed-surface riding, because that is not the happy place for this suspension or bike.

Although I mentioned some of the drawbacks of the 100mm suspension, I don’t really think that stuff is a big deal. You want that suspension because you want the traction. What actually does bother me is the lack of saddle-to-bar drop. It’s inherent to any 100mm suspension and fixing it is tricky, but if I could wave my wand and fix something, it would be this.

The reason it bugs me is that I want a bike that feels fast. When I really want to push hard, I am used to tucking in, getting aero, and just pedaling. In the case of the Pivot Les SL, it feels impossible to match that feeling because it’s so upright and the bars are super wide. Sure, I could swap the bars, but getting that long and low feeling is a bit more tricky.

The reason the problem exists is that 100mm of travel requires more space. The axle-to-crown length on a fork with this much travel pushes the front end up higher than a standard rigid gravel bike. While Pivot keeps the head tube as short as possible to compensate, you are still left with very little saddle-to-bar drop. Unless you are willing to swap in a radically negative-angled stem to slam the bars, you are going to be sitting relatively upright. It is a necessary compromise to fit that much suspension on a frame, but the result is a bike that feels incredibly capable in the rough, but somewhat sluggish and blocky when you are just trying to put your head down and crush a smooth fire road. This detail is why you sometimes see drop-bar conversions with bonkers-looking negative stems.

Unlike the 100mm suspension fork, I don’t believe this upright posture is really the point of the bike. While it is true that an upright position adds stability, if the bar and stem managed to get the racy position I like and I could combine that with the 100mm of travel, this bike would feel a whole lot different. It would shift the use case a little more toward gravel roads, but I would personally have a lot more fun riding it.…

title: Billionaire tax: how a union leader’s ‘crazy’ idea became the defining issue of California’s midterms
author: Dara Kerr
text:
It was an ambitious notion – now Californians will vote on a one-time 5% billionaire tax, and state’s super rich have pulled out all the stops in opposition

One year ago, the idea of a billionaire tax in California was still in its infancy.

It wasn’t yet one of the most contentious ballot measure fights in state history – pitting Democrats against Democrats, drawing national attention from political heavyweights, and netting hundreds of millions of Silicon Valley dollars to fight it. Back then, it was a bold and desperate answer to Donald Trump’s healthcare cuts.

Trump had just signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which dictated a trillion dollars of Medicaid, Affordable Care Act and other healthcare funding be cut over the next decade to offset sweeping tax cuts. When the bill goes into effect in January, that could mean more than 3.4m Californians will lose their coverage, including millions of children.

“That’s why we were willing to do something that lots of people said was crazy,” said Dave Regan, the divisive architect of the billionaire tax and president of the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW). “To us, what’s crazy is doing nothing and watching millions of people lose coverage.”

Now, with the midterms less than a week away, California voters will decide on whether to pass the ballot measure known as Proposition 40. The proposal would levy a one-time 5% tax on billionaires living in the state as of 1 January 2026, the proceeds of which would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.

The initiative has its critics, even among Democrats, who point at its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. But its most vocal critics have been billionaires.

The idea of taxing the Golden State’s ultra-wealthy has snowballed into a messy brawl over the last year. Progressive politicians have become bedfellows with tech billionaires, opposition ballot measure campaigns have been mounted, Signal chats leaked, and boatloads of money have been spent.

Tech billionaires have treated the proposal as an existential threat, dumping upwards of $356m into “independent expenditure-only” political action committees (Super Pacs) to stop it. In the first two weeks of October, according to the most recent campaign filings, the opposition campaign spent more than $42.8m – surpassing $2.5m per day. That money went to an army of consultants , who have been tasked with lobbying politicians, blanketing the airwaves with ads and placing op-eds in Latino newspapers across the state.

“This looks like it’s going to be the most expensive ballot measure ever,” said David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University. “Not in California history, but in the history of the world.”

Meanwhile, the far-less-funded pro-Prop 40 camp has relied on viral social media campaigns from influencers and actors, including the artist Shepard Fairey and actor Mark Ruffalo , and raucous rallies headlined by leftwing politicians. During one packed event in San Francisco earlier this month, Vermont’s Bernie Sanders said: “The whole country, and frankly people from around the world, are paying attention to what is happening here.”

While Prop 40 is just one ballot measure election in one state, it is causing ripple effects nationwide. It comes at a time when affordability is top of mind and the disparity of wealth in the US hasn’t been so stark since the Great Depression . McCuan said the billionaires’ big spend was partially due to a fear of contagion to other states. Likewise, supporters say they hope the proposed tax is a harbinger for referendums on wealth inequality across the country.

Regan and his union got started on their endeavor last summer. After Trump signed his bill on 4 July, Regan’s team began making calls. They put together a working group of policy experts, economists, lawyers, researchers and political consultants, who came up with the one-time 5% tax to keep hospitals open and union healthcare workers in their jobs.

Regan is known for using the ballot measure process as a political tool to strongarm deals with lawmakers and push causes important to the SEIU-UHW. Since 2012, the union has sponsored 48 initiatives . The strategy with the billionaire tax was to sharpen the focus on inequality.

“We worked to come up with something that could draw enough support from voters, and that could avoid a catastrophe,” Regan said. “We just bore down on that.”

When their plan became public after the October 2025 filing deadline, the billionaires hatched a working group of their own.

Chris Larsen, a cryptocurrency mogul, hosted a Christmas party in northern California’s swanky Marin county last December, according to Bloomberg . It was in a treehouse tucked into a grove of towering redwood trees. The singer Janelle Monáe performed and California governor Gavin Newsom was there, along with Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

Newsom’s relationship with Brin goes back decades to when he was mayor of San Francisco. The governor, now a presumed presidential candidate, had flown on Google’s jet with Brin , and the two men attended each other’s weddings. But a lengthy exchange they reportedly had at Larsen’s party was far from collegial.

Brin confronted Newsom about the proposed billionaire tax, according to people who spoke with Newsom, Bloomberg reported. The Google co-founder, currently worth about $245bn, told the governor it was forcing him to leave California.

Newsom and Brin did not respond to the Guardian’s detailed list of questions.…

title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Mickey Rivers
author: Andrew Mearns
text:
Decades before Yankees fan favorites like Bernie Williams and Brett Gardner patrolled center field, the team featured another player who could really move: Mickey Rivers. He only played three and a half seasons with the Yankees, but “Mick the Quick” instantly became a fan favorite for his solid production as the leadoff hitter for three American League pennant-winning squads and two World Series champions.

John Milton “Mickey” Rivers : October 30, 1948 (Miami, FL): 1976-79

Somewhat amusingly, Rivers actually got the nickname “Mickey” for his resemblance to his Aunt Mickey. He developed incredible speed in his youth with the Northwestern High School Bulls in Miami, lettering in baseball, track, football, and basketball before graduating from there in ‘67. Rivers moved on to Miami Dade College for a couple seasons, coincidentally playing alongside future Yankees teammate Bucky Dent. He became one of the finest Junior College players in history, later being named in 1999 to the National Junior College All-Century Team and the Florida Community College All-Time team.

Major League Baseball did multiple drafts per year at this time, and Rivers was drafted out of college four separate times from January of ’68 through June of ’69 by the White Sox, Mets, Senators, and ultimately, the Braves. Rivers held out long enough to play for the team closest to home, but it would not last. After hitting .307/.464/.511 with 31 steals in 67 games on the Pioneer League’s Magic Valley Cowboys, Rivers was traded for the first of three times in his career. Atlanta sought pitching help down the stretch as they sought to clinch their first division title since the move from Milwaukee in ’66, so the 20-year-old was off to Anaheim and the California Angels along with pitching prospect Clint Compton in a September 8th deal for veteran knuckleballer Hoyt Wilhelm and Bob Priddy.

Rivers spent the offseason with the Puerto Rican Winter League’s Santurce Crabbers, then jumped to Double-A El Paso at the start of the ‘70 season. He dominated the Texas League with a .343/.426/.537 triple slash, impressing the Angels enough to earn a promotion by the end of the season to the majors at age 21. Rivers split parts of the next three seasons between Salt Lake City and the Angels, clearly outclassing his peers in Triple-A, but never impressing any of the three managers to skipper the Angels from ‘71-‘73. In the final month of ‘73 though, he hit .349/.391/.457 in 141 plate appearances with eight stolen bases in 30 games. Manager Bobby Winkles’ eyes were finally opened to Rivers, and he spent all of ‘74 in the majors.

Across his first two full seasons, Rivers hit .285/.335/.373 with a 109 OPS+ and 6.8 rWAR. However, the leadoff hitter’s breakneck speed is what really made him stand out–he led the AL in triples with 11 in 118 games in ‘74, then led the majors in triple with 13 in ‘75. He finished sixth in the AL in steals in ‘74 with 30 before far surpassing that with a league-high and career-high 70 in ‘75 — still the Halos’ all-time record. Outside of Bert Campaneris and Luis Aparicio, the stolen base had become a lost art in the AL since the end of the Deadball Era; Rivers was only the second AL player to notch 70 steals in a 60-year stretch dating back to Ty Cobb’s 96 in 1915.

Yankees team president and general manager Gabe Paul had a team that contended in ’75, but could not catch up to the division-winning Red Sox. Thanks to assistant and future Hall of Fame GM Pat Gillick, Paul was able to turn the overachievers on his ’75 squad into multiple players through trades. On December 11th, he pulled off two trades that would make a huge impact on Billy Martin’s team. Starter Doc Medich was sent to the Pirates for pitchers Ken Brett and Dock Ellis in addition to unheralded second baseman Willie Randolph, and 30/30 outfielder Bobby Bonds was dealt to the Angels for Rivers and starter Ed Figueroa. Bonds impressed the Yankees in his only season with them following the controversial Bobby Murcer-for-Bobby Bonds deal, but management expressed concerns over Bonds’ alcoholism. Thus, the Yankees had their third All-Star-caliber center fielder in three years.

Rivers had actually never been named to the Midsummer Classic before, but a strong .310/.322/.448 first half with 20 doubles and 25 stolen bases earned him the only All-Star selection of his career. He proved to be the igniter the Yankees needed at the top of the batting order that year, and while he did not steal nearly as many bases as he did in ‘75, his 43 steals in 50 attempts led to a league-best 86-percent stolen base rate. Rivers also played better defense than he ever had before in his career, leading to a 6.3 rWAR season in total (fifth in the AL). He finished third in AL MVP voting for his outstanding efforts and the Yankees won the AL East to clinch their first playoff berth in 12 years. The Yankees actually voted Rivers team MVP over his teammate and captain, Thurman Munson, despite the fact that the latter was the winner of the AL MVP. The long wait plagued by horrid baseball in wake of the Stengel/Houk dynasty years was over.

The Yankees faced the Kansas City Royals in the ALCS, who were making the first playoff appearance in franchise history. Rivers had a multi-hit game in the opener, and both times, the Yankees’ offense brought him home; they won 4-1. The Royals cooled him off in the next three games, holding him to two singles and a walk in 14 plate appearances, helping them knot the series and bring it to a decisive Game 5. Rivers came up big in this must-win game, going 4-for-5 with a triple with three runs scored out of the Yankees’ seven. When cleanup hitter Chris Chambliss’ solo homer off Mark Littell sailed over the wall in the bottom of the ninth, bedlam erupted. The Yankees were going to the World Series and Rivers was off to his first Fall Classic.

The World Series was a huge letdown from the exciting ALCS. The Cincinnati Reds’ dominant “Big Red Machine” destroyed the Yankees in a four-game sweep. The fact that Reds pitchers limited Rivers to just a trio of hits in 18 plate appearances was crucial to their victory. During this time, Rivers’ off-the-field problems really started to crop up. He would gamble away his paycheck almost immediately after receiving it, and his wife Mary even requested that George Steinbrenner mail his checks directly to her. In the middle of the World Series, she took her wrath out on Rivers in the Yankees’ parking lot, where she literally played bumper cars. It was a terrible distraction to the team and drove Steinbrenner nuts.

On the plus side, Rivers had a season nearly as great as his ’76 in ’77, accompanied by another stellar performance in the ALCS against Kansas City. He pummeled Royals pitching for nine hits and a .391 average as the Yankees proceeded to their second consecutive World Series.

Rivers slumped again to a .222/.222/.296 triple slash against the Dodgers, but he did have a defensive highlight in throwing Steve Garvey out at the plate in the opener . The Yankees prevailed to win it all behind World Series MVP Reggie Jackson. Rivers and Jackson had an interesting dynamic together. Jackson told reporters one time that Rivers should learn how to read and write, to which Rivers replied, “You’d better stop readin’ and writing’ and start hittin’!” On another occasion, Jackson told reporters that he had an IQ of 160, and Rivers quipped back, “Out of what, a thousand?”

Rivers slumped to slightly below league average offensively in ‘78, especially struggling as the Yankees fell 14.5 games behind the Red Sox in the AL East. In the second half though, he recovered with an improved .270/.309/.410 triple slash, featuring 19 doubles and 15 steals. He was even better in the playoffs when the Yankees passed the Red Sox to capture the AL East in a one-game playoff. Rivers had his finest overall postseason to date, batting .379/.419/.379 in nine games, finally complementing another superb ALCS (.455/.538/.455 in four games) with a solid World Series against the Dodgers. Rivers was a champion for the second time in his career.

Rivers was off to another mediocre start in ’79 (98 OPS+), and on August 1st, the Yankees dealt away their embattled center fielder to the Texas Rangers in an eight-player deal to reacquire Oscar Gamble. He was still a decent player, but the Yankees had grown tired of his off-the-field problems, and they longed to bring Rivers’ former teammate Gamble back after letting him go following his ’76 season. The deal worked out for both teams, as Gamble played five and a half more years in New York with a 143 OPS+ (albeit somewhat part-time), and Rivers set the Rangers’ single-season record for hits in 1980 with 210, a mark that lasted for 35 years until Michael Young broke it with 221 in 2005. Texas baseball writers selected him as the Rangers’ Player of the Year in ’80.

Rivers hit .303/.327/.397 over the next five and a half seasons with the Rangers, but his caliber of play precipitously fell after his age-32 season in ‘81. His amusing line about season goals of “hitting .300, scoring 100 runs, and staying injury-prone,” was only 33 percent fulfilled … by the last “goal.” His speed declined, as he only stole 48 bases throughout his Texas career, and he played only 115 games from ‘82-‘83. After a modest comeback to a 93 OPS+ in 102 games in ‘84, he called it quits at age 35. Rivers retired as a .295/.327/.397 hitting in 1,468 games over 15 seasons with 267 stolen bases and 32.3 rWAR to his name.

Since retiring, Rivers returned home to Florida, where he brought his interest of racehorses to a healthier state, preferring to raise them rather than gamble away his earnings on them. He’s been a constant presence at Old Timers’ Day since ‘88 (when he amusingly only 39), and he was inducted into the Texas Baseball Hall of Fame in ‘95. Bill James ranked Rivers the 59th-greatest center fielder in MLB history in his 2002 Historical Baseball Abstract. We placed him 92nd on our most recent edition of the top Yankees in franchise history.

Rivers had quite the up-and-down Yankees tenure, but throughout it all, he was a crucial addition to the Yankees’ lineup. Without their sparkplug, it’s unclear whether or not the Yankees could have reached the great heights as back-to-back champions in the late-‘70s.

Here’s hoping that the 1978 champion “Mick the Quick” has an appropriately wonderful 78th birthday!
