title: Is virtual racing 'real' racing? – Our team weighs in on whether esports is 'legit' or 'just a fitness contest'
author: cyclingnews@cyclingnews.com (Cyclingnews)
text:
Back in the day, the prospect of an indoor turbo trainer session (that's what we called them before they got smart, kids) would generally unite cyclists, who pretty much unanimously agreed that they were a great way of getting a quality session in, but they were hard and generally a means to an end, that being improved fitness and form.

With the rise of smart trainers and everything that comes with them, from virtual mountain climbing to intense virtual e-racing, opinions on the latter seem to be a bit more skewed.

Some riders, particularly in winter, get stuck into virtual racing to maintain fitness, whilst others shun any sort of virtual world and simply head out in the wet and cold to train.

Virtual racing has only grown in recent years; there's a rainbow jersey for it now, and the inaugural UCI Esports World Championship took place back in December 2020. It can also be incredibly lucrative, with big prize pots up for grabs on a regular basis.

But does virtual racing really count? It's Indoor Cycling Week at , and the team got together for another editors' roundtable for a healthy exchange of views on the legitimacy of racing indoors.

Here are our thoughts, but let us know yours too. Is virtual racing real racing?

Is there a treadmill world championship? No, exactly.

I could probably stop there, as I think that summarises my point quite well. To me, indoor racing lacks all of the things that make cycling truly competitive. It's a test of fitness, sure (and a difficult one at that; I don't doubt indoor athletes are incredibly strong), but the element of tactics, gameplay, positioning and, to be frank, racing skill is so minimal that it feels very far removed from actual racing.

It's also more or less completely useless as a spectator event, which I think is a key element of being a sport – there has to be a degree of entertainment.

To me, indoor competition is more akin to the Hyrox world championships or a fitness contest than real bike racing. Challenging and a big achievement for the competitors, yes, but a real sport that the public need particularly pay attention to? Not really.

Virtual racing, as Matilda already pointed out, is racing in the way a swim meet is racing. But if rubbing is racing, it's definitely not.

You can't throw an elbow, dive the inside of a turn, latch onto another team's lead-out train or use your descending skills to get away from your competition (see Chris Froome/Col de Peyresourde, Matej Mohorič/Sanremo, Marianne Vos/Giro).

Real racing takes skill, tactical nous, teamwork and luck – all aspects absent in virtual racing. But if you consider a VO2 max test to be 'real racing', then, sure.

Of course, virtual racing is real racing.

I haven’t raced a bike for real in a very long time, and there’s no way I’ll go back to it. I wasn’t very good – though I did once win a race – I’m no longer very fit, and even in veterans racing, the variation of ability in the real sport is huge.

With online racing you actually race against others of around the same physical ability, which suits me. That said, I’ve only done it once, and then only to test a power meter, but it was short, sweet, incredibly hard, great fun, and Zwift awarded me a new FTP after I came second.

And for all those efforts on the road or in any other indoor session, I can never push myself as hard as when there’s the thrill of competition.

I’ll certainly give it another go, maybe in the next month or so.

No. In much the same way that rowing on an erg machine in the gym doesn’t give you the spray of delicious river water (or sewage, depending on which water company’s area you’re operating in), riding indoors totally fails to offer anything close to the experience of riding and racing outside.

Can I take that corner faster, or will the tyres slide? The wind has changed direction. I can’t see; there’s too much grit in my eyes. Indoor racing is sanitised nonsense, and I’d be just as happy having a test to see who has the highest FTP and be done with it, as bike racing without bike handling is just a fitness test.

Of course it's real racing. The finish line might be made out of pixels, but if racing on Zwift isn't real racing, then neither is Mario Kart, and I think we all know that it is.

Sure, it's not the same as outdoor racing, and it's not a spectator sport. But when I'm being dropped from the lead group on a climb, that feels pretty damn realistic.

Can indoor bicycle racing be considered real racing? The 'indoor trainer' remains just that: a fitness tool, not a race machine. Akin to my lovely NordicTrack, which still gets used occasionally, there is no virtual classic cross-country skiing championship, or skimo or even biathlon (can you imagine?).

I do think the training apps that allow people to test their skills against each other bring the feel of a peloton, but it is not a real race. Besides, the true definition of 'peloton' – a group moving forward – just doesn't ring true for stationary bikes.

Indoor racing is real racing.

Indoor racing can be shockingly hard; suffering and pushing as hard as you can whilst sitting on a stationary bike indoors is really tough. Indoor racing and efforts demand a special kind of suffering, and it definitely counts.

I see indoor racing sitting off to one side; I’m never going to love it or see it the same way as I see road, or any other kind of real-world racing, but I have respect for the world's best indoor racers; they are putting out incredible numbers and performances indoors, and that takes a certain type of rider and skill set. The effort is very real.

Indoor racing also has nuance and tactics that can’t be overlooked; it’s improved as online platforms and technology have developed over time.

Indoor racing is legit, but don’t count your indoor kilometres as real ones – they don’t count!

The appeal of the bike for me is intrinsically tied to the outdoors, with the unpredictability and sense of discovery of the world around me crucial to my enjoyment of the sport, both as a rider and spectator.

That means even track cycling fails to connect in the same way, and virtual racing takes that to a whole other level. Still, while I'm not drawn to virtual racing and struggle to connect with it, I can't dismiss it. The effort and competitive sensations are all real and also I can see how virtual training and racing can be such a valuable tool to close some of the vast chasms in opportunity.

The clincher for me is that Australians Jay Vine, Neve Bradbury and Emily Dixon are unquestionably real racers, and they gained their opportunity to enter the pro ranks , despite the geographical hurdles they faced, via a virtual training and racing platform.

It's hard to question the validity of a racing medium where talent like that rises to the top. So, yes, virtual racing is real racing, but just please don't make me watch it.

If the objective is to get from point A to point B first, then I will call it a race every single time.

Yes, virtual racing is real racing. It certainly lacks elements and variables compared to racing on the road, trails, track, etc., but it requires training in strength, endurance, tactics, and skill - even if it is taking place inside of a gaming world.

For a lot of athletes, racing is largely a mental battle that is won in the mind first, with drive, focus, confidence, visualisation and the ability to push past limits while under pressure, whether it's on the road or a virtual platform.

While there is no treadmill World Championships (yet), there is treadmill racing; ask Eric Min, who caught me right on the finish line for third place in a Zwift race … I'll get him next time we line up on the starting line.

Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. title: Britain’s blighted high streets will improve by next election, says Rayner
author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
text:
Housing secretary says Labour wants to reverse fortunes of towns plagued by boarded-up shops and rogue businesses

Angela Rayner has said voters will begin to see a difference in their high street before the next general election as Labour prioritises investment in struggling local communities.

The housing secretary said the government had made it a top priority before the country goes to the polls to begin turning around the fortunes of places blighted by boarded-up shops and rogue businesses.

“There’s been a real sense of decline,” she said. “People see it as part of the identity of their town and area, and that’s why we’ve got our high streets strategy.”

Speaking after John Healey, the chancellor, earmarked more than £1bn in his debut budget on Wednesday to support retail, hospitality and leisure businesses, Rayner signalled that the government stood ready to take further action.

“The chancellor has shown he’s backing our high streets, backing our businesses that have been struggling and giving them the breathing space,” she said. “And he’s going to continue with that.”

In an interview for the Guardian’s series on the fortunes of Britain’s towns, Rayner insisted that the budget was “moving the needle” for the economy as she sought to defend Healey from criticism.

On Thursday the chancellor was warned by the Resolution Foundation and the Institute for Fiscal Studies that his measures were poorly targeted and had paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year.

Meanwhile, the owners of Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators , putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk in a blow for towns across the country where the discount chain is a high street fixture.

Speaking before that announcement, Rayner said the government was taking action to ease the pressure on businesses and households amid the damage to Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

“All these businesses that people value, that make up a thriving high street, the chancellor is really giving them support,” she said.

Asked whether voters would be able to see a difference in their local shopping districts before the next general election, she said: “The money will start to come through. Already we’ve put the £5.8bn in.

“Next year, from April, business rates [cuts] will apply and you’ll see [other] money in more areas.”

On his way to becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged a new dawn for Britain’s high streets , placing the revival of overlooked town centres at the heart of his agenda for government.

In response to this agenda, Healey said he would cut business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure companies in a plan worth £1bn over two years, with the relief partly funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops.

Labour also launched a revamped “hope on the high street” strategy alongside the chancellor’s budget to coordinate investment and the transfer of power to local leaders. This includes the already announced £5.8bn “pride in place” programme to support regeneration projects and £210m fund to transform derelict buildings .

“There’s a lot of money and funding pots going into the high street, as well as work in the public realm to deliver services and housing,” Rayner said.

However, business leaders said more fundamental changes to the business rates system were needed, highlighting that Labour had promised to replace it entirely in its manifesto.

Before the budget Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, told the Guardian that changes to tax online sales at higher rates than in-store purchases were needed to help “level the playing field” for struggling bricks-and-mortar stores.

Hinting at further changes to come, budget documents show ministers are exploring “how the business rates system could better target online retailers in ways that minimise any indirect impacts for wider retail businesses” to fund support for the high street.

Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
text:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what could be the largest hack in history.

The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".

Early checks show the incident may have involved an engineer's laptop that had been compromised, which allowed an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.

Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025 , to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.

AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.

The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.

The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.

Chainalysis, another crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.

Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets.

Binance did not directly respond to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue.

In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.

"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said.

Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they have frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.

Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said his firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident.

Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies.

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen around $1.6bn "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."

"Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," said Ardoino, whose company issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds.

Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.

Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.

Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.

The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under custody.

Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

title: Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
text:
Oxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil Shamsan

The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.

Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.

The city’s daily minimum water needs are estimated at about 35,000 cubic metres, he said, but no more than 1,000 cubic metres was being allowed to reach it each day and that water shipments were being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city.

With food stocks depleted and the price of wheat soaring, he said “citizens are heading back to the stone age”. Restaurants had closed due to the lack of fuel.

Shamsan said that as many as 1,800 people were in need of dialysis treatment but were unable to access supplies, that 120 health centres had been suspended and schools had closed, affecting hundreds of thousands of children.

He said 64 people had been killed, including civilians, from August to 20 October 2026 and a further 173 injured. More than 6,400 newly displaced families, each averaging seven members, had come to the city to flee the fighting.

“We are not talking about living, just surviving,” he said.

His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”

Shamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.

He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.

People in occupied territories were being required to show loyalty to the Zaydi religion and to sign forms affirming they had joined the Houthis. “They are not starting a war but an revolution in identity,” Shamsan said, adding that scores of children from each village were being forcibly ordered without their parents’ consent to join the frontlines in Saada and elsewhere.

Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.

Shamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.

Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.

“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”

title: ‘You can see the water going down’: residents on edge as one of England’s worst-hit reservoirs dries up
author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
text:
After UK’s hottest summer on record, Ardingly near Haywards Heath is just 19% full – and next-closest reservoir is unusable due to broken treatment works

“Y ou can see the water level at Ardingly going down and down. I don’t remember ever seeing it this low,” says Caroline Allan, a lifetime resident of Haywards Heath, the nearest town to one of England’s most depleted reservoirs.

The Ardingly reservoir, managed by South East Water and serving about 95,000 properties in and around Haywards Heath and Uckfield in Sussex, is currently 19% full.

The day the Guardian visited, the weather was grey and rainy, incongruous with the muddy reservoir bed that should have been submerged under six metres of water.

Earlier this month a severe drought was declared in parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex, with urgent measures being taken to secure public water supplies after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record .

Severe drought is the highest level of drought and is declared when evidence shows drought is causing or will soon cause serious harm, and when emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services.

“They will probably never lift the hosepipe ban and it just seems so unfair that they’re making the area more and more crowded but they’re not increasing the capacity to store water,” said Allan.

There has been a steady stream of new housing developments around Haywards Heath, sparking local opposition , with concerns that a growing local population is putting pressure on already strained resources.

Water demand is increasing as the population grows and new industrial demands from datacentres and energy infrastructure require more water. Plus, the water available to supply those needs is reducing as the climate crisis worsens, resulting in greater variability and unpredictability of rainfall and greater water demand during hotter, drier summers. There has also been a lack of investment over several decades in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs.

Most of Europe has endured back-to-back climate crisis-driven heatwaves this summer. The extreme heat, coupled with little rainfall, means 82% of England and large parts of Wales are still in drought or severe drought.

The Environment Agency would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of year and yet supplies at several reservoirs are critically low. This includes Ardingly and Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers and is 14.5% full.

It is estimated that 120% of average rainfall is needed between now and April for all areas to be considered out of drought. The government’s national drought group was told on Wednesday that despite the “weather whiplash” brought by Storm Austen and Boelo , the recent rain has not changed the drought outlook.

Less than six miles away from Ardingly, Southern Water’s Weir Wood reservoir is 80% full because a water treatment works at the site has been out of action since 2018.

“It’s crazy that they’ve got Weir Wood next door and they’re not using it. I think that’s madness,” Allan said.

Graham Ward, who has lived in Haywards Heath for his whole life, also said it was “crazy” that there was a full neighbouring reservoir that cannot be used.

During the drought in 2025, South East Water announced emergency plans to connect the Ardingly and Weir Wood reservoirs together by an overground pipeline. When the rain came and the drought conditions eased, these plans were shelved.

Southern Water is now seeking to rebuild the treatment works at Weir Wood by 2030, and South East Water is conducting a feasibility study of a buried pipeline to connect the two reservoirs.

But after government guidance to stockpile essential goods , water scarcity has become a pressing concern for local residents. “We’re really not that far away from Weir Wood, and we’ve got Ardingly with hardly any water in it and we’re told to buy water. It’s just crazy,” said Allan.

Ward said he has already been storing water for some time in anticipation.

“I am worried, but I also think there should be responsibility on the water companies to get the reservoirs working as they should be. The infrastructure is crumbling and it’s not fit for purpose any more; if we continually have hot summers, this is going to be a problem every year,” he said.

Delphine Hazeldon, who has lived in Haywards Heath for more than 20 years, also said she has never seen the Ardingly reservoir so low.

“Our relatives in Australia, they’re always asking for updates and they’re horrified. It is a definite worry, we’re approaching 80, but we think well, it’ll be our children and our children’s children facing the problem. The whole thing is a mess.”

A spokesperson at Southern Water said: “Weir Wood reservoir is being rebuilt to ensure long-term water resilience for the North Sussex region, in the face of climate change and population growth. The existing treatment works date from the 1950s and reached the end of its operational life, with significant reliability and water-quality challenges. The site was therefore taken out of supply in 2018. “While a number of options were considered, a complete rebuild was identified as the best long-term solution to provide a reliable and resilient water supply for customers in the area. While we already supply water to South East Water through an existing interconnected network, Ardingly’s current situation would not be resolved if Weir Wood treatment works were operational.”

Water minister, Emma Hardy, who chaired a national drought group meeting on Wednesday, said: “Despite the recent rain, the situation remains serious. As we move through autumn and winter, we now face the challenge of having drought and flood simultaneously as the rain struggles to be absorbed by the hardened ground.…

title: MotoGP Malaysian GP: Marquez tops practice as Martin ends Friday early
How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
text:
The moment she saw footage from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Kacey Doran picked up her phone. She had to tell her sister.

"Have you seen this?" messaged Doran, excitedly.

Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. Ocarina's fantasy-like story, and beautiful music, enthralled them both.

It was also the first game Doran ever completed. Now, countless memories rushed back to her as she devoured clips of the fully redesigned version, due to arrive on the Switch 2 later this year.

Doran's sister messaged back: "I'm not tearing up… YOU'RE tearing up."

This is the power of nostalgia – and a perfect example of how video games can trigger it. Doran now teaches an esports course at Rowan University in New Jersey. She says the original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, had a "magical" quality that she hopes to rediscover, and also share with her sister's children.

The video games industry has long leaned on remakes. From Mario Kart to the Final Fantasy series, or even Pac-Man, some games just keep coming back in updated forms, as new generations of gamers emerge and as computer hardware improves, enabling more detailed graphics and increasingly expansive game worlds.

While the emotional hook may be the most significant draw, putting out a remake can be a double-edged sword. Some gamers are very protective of their favourite titles and new versions don't always meet certain fans' astronomically high expectations.

Nostalgia is an important but mixed emotion, says Tim Wulf, at the Centre for Advanced Internet Studies in Bochum, Germany. It has positive aspects but also a kind of sadness, too. Happiness in remembering things that were important to us, and also an awareness that that time is now gone.

"It's a social emotion because memories that induce nostalgia for us are connected to other people," he explains, adding that nostalgia can boost our self-esteem while highlighting key social bonds.

Video games, says Wulf, are notoriously good at triggering nostalgia because gamers can "jump into the same environment". In other words, games are like time machines for our emotions, and returning to fondly remembered places can feel stabilising or reassuring in an ever-changing world.

Doran, for one, notes that when you return to a favourite old game, there's something satisfying about deploying previously learned skills. You know what to do here, you're winning again. Just like the old days.

Putting out remasters and remakes has been a "really successful" strategy for the games industry, says Piers Harding-Rolls, head of games research at Ampere Analysis.

"Tying in with established audiences and building on existing content is quite a safe route for a lot of companies," he adds. In many cases, it is cheaper to update an existing game rather than create a new title from scratch.

Among other remakes that have found big audiences recently are those of Resident Evil 4 and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.

But Ocarina of Time perhaps stands out because, ever since its original release, it has been considered by many as one of the greatest games ever made. "The interest from all the Gen Zs that I work with is really high," says Harding-Rolls. The legend of The Legend of Zelda, as it were.

Clearly, nostalgia is not the only driver of interest in the remake, and today's audiences will expect a game that plays to today's standards.

Games companies must keep innovating when linking contemporary audiences to the past, says Wulf, in order satisfy their desire for fresh experiences. And although Wulf himself was a big fan of the original, he has no personal interest in the Ocarina of Time remake. "I want a new game – I don't want to play an old game," he says. Nostalgia isn't always enough for some.

Plus, critics often highlight a tension between originals and remakes. Which is the definitive version? In 2021, Square Enix released the bizarrely titled Nier Replicant ver.1.22474487139... – a remaster of a game first published in 2010. One reviewer wrote , external , "What we're left with is two nearly identical Niers each vying to be the true Nier."

Fans may react badly should a remaster or remake fail to do justice to the source material. And, in the gaming world, angry fan reactions can be serious .

"There's always going to be that fan base or group of people that are going to nit-pick," says Stephanie Ijoma, chief executive and founder of NNESAGA, a consultancy and creative agency.

Ultimately, games developers working on remakes have to "find the right balance" between appealing to fans and allowing themselves to be creative with the material, she adds. "You can't make art in fear, you can't create in fear."

Ijoma gives the example of Final Fantasy VII. First released in 1997, it got a highly anticipated remake in 2020.

This was a game Ijoma played back in the late 1990s and she was thrilled to be able to share it with younger players today.

Remakes enable this sharing of experiences because getting old computer hardware or video games consoles to work, while a pastime loved by some , is not possible for everyone.

"I've tried multiple times to play Silent Hill 2 because I'm interested in older games but it's such a difficult game to come into nowadays," says Niklas Hallin, a solo indie game developer who runs the studio Neckbolt. "They made a remake and it's so smooth, it just works. It works on your modern hardware."

Hallin did not play many games as a child so he says nostalgia isn't much of a motivator for him. However, in his own games, he likes to include subtle stylistic references to classic games because he knows that this appeals to gamers.…

title: F1 has never had anyone like me - Hamilton
text:
Lewis Hamilton says he is unlike any driver Formula 1 has seen before and reaffirmed a determination to keep racing into his mid-forties.

The seven-time world champion recently said he wanted to continue in the sport to fulfil a dream of racing in Africa, having campaigned for a Grand Prix there for many years.

F1 has signed a 10-year deal with the central-east African country of Rwanda starting in the early 2030s which will be a first race on the continent since 1993.

The Briton said F1 had "never had anyone like me in the 70 years" of the sport and he felt like he was "built differently".

Hamilton will be at least 45 when that race takes place - the same age as Aston Martin driver Fernando Alonso, who is continuing in F1 next year - but he told a news conference before this weekend's Mexico Grand Prix that he should be considered a special case.

"Of course there are challenges up ahead that I can't foresee that come with age. But along this journey there have been so many pre-conceived ideas like that your reaction time drops off," he said.

"Did you see my reaction time in the last race? It was faster than some of the youngest people here.

"As long as you are willing to sacrifice everything, which I am right now – I can't say in four years whether I will want to continue doing what I'm doing – but I am still all in. I will be for the foreseeable future."

Approach African GP with humility, says Hamilton

Alonso turns 46 next summer, and hinted when he announced his new contract last month that he is likely to continue for at least another season beyond that .

Hamilton is battling to finish second in the drivers' championship this season.

The Ferrari driver is in a fight with four other drivers to end the season behind runaway leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes, who is 21 years Hamilton's junior.

Antonelli is poised to clinch his first world title this weekend in Mexico City , while there are just 31 points separating Mercedes' George Russell in second from McLaren's Lando Norris in sixth.

Hamilton is third, one point behind Russell, five ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and eight ahead of the other Ferrari driver, Charles Leclerc.

Hamilton struggled during his first season with Ferrari, but has enjoyed a much more positive campaign this time around including victory in the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix in June.

Hamilton said he has proven that he can still compete at the highest level.

"Time will tell whether I'm here in the 2030s. I never want to overstay my welcome in the sense of not having the performance," he added.

"I don't want to be driving around with that having really dropped off.

"Everyone assumed that last year and I have proved everyone wrong. I'll continue to try to do so."

title: P&R urged to speed up review of relocation grants
text:
Guernsey's top political committee is being urged to prioritise a review of relocation allowances amid concerns it is putting pressure on rental prices.

Policy and Resources (P&R) said in June last year , external the review was "on track" to be finished by the end of September 2025.

Deputy Tom Rylatt, from Forward Guernsey, said the review should "be a priority for P&R" and the delay was disappointing.

P&R President Lindsay de Sausmarez said "several stages of work on the review have been completed" and the committee was due to consider it again shortly.

She blamed the delay on how busy the committee had been recently including delivering reforms to the island's tax system and a budget for 2027 .

A recent report from the Scutiny Management Committee , external linked the relocation allowances to the current high price of renting a home in Guernsey.

The current policy , external entitles people relocating to Guernsey for jobs with the States of Guernsey to a £5,000 grant (£6,600 for Alderney) alongside help with rental costs for up to four years, storage costs and, in some cases, support with an unsold home's mortgage.

In the last decade rents have risen by 65% to on average £2,138 per month, according to the States of Guernsey , external .

A freedom of information request earlier this year revealed more than £5m was spent by the States on relocation packages in 2025, the most since the support was introduced.

Deputy Rylatt said: "It is disappointing that the review has still not been completed, having originally been due in September 2025.

"With housing costs continuing to place enormous pressure on islanders, it needs to be a priority for P&R that we understand the impact these packages may be having, particularly on the rental market.

"I hope the committee will now bring this work to a conclusion and set out what changes, if any, it intends to make."

Those buying a home in Guernsey can also qualify for a £8,750 house purchase grant, while short-term recruits could receive smaller payments towards travel and moving costs.

Scrutiny Management Committee President Andy Sloan said the current policy was "excessive" and believes "such a subsidy is likely to have an upward impact on local market rents".

In June 2025 P&R said the review of these grants would look at different options for relocation support, including possible alternatives, using workforce data and financial analysis.

It said any changes would need to balance potential savings against the need to recruit and retain staff in essential public services such as health, education, social care and law enforcement.

Officials said the review was unlikely to be made public as it was looking at an internal policy but any changes would be clearly communicated by P&R.

title: How talking about Man Utd's cycle of doom became an industry
text:
Manchester United . More a high-volume content farm than a football club these days.

Michael Carrick's starring role in what has become one of the nation's favourite soap operas has been extended for at least another week, with the 45-year-old set to be in charge for Saturday's visit to Chelsea .

Good news - you'd think - for Carrick. But even better news for Amazon's All or Nothing camera crews, who have been given "unprecedented" access to document the behind-the-scenes goings-on at Old Trafford this season.

United fans will presumably be relieved when the football resumes on Saturday, if only to break up the constant stream of opinion for 90 minutes.

But while the wall-to-wall reporting of one of the world's biggest football clubs is hardly new, the unrelenting coverage from former players is a growing phenomenon.

It is easier to name the Manchester United legends who don't have a platform from which they scrutinise the club's every move than those that do - and it begs the question whether the club's demise has been industrialised into a content-creating machine.

Whether supporters feel comments from ex-players are damaging or not differs from fan to fan, but what cannot be denied is how difficult it is to escape their views.

Sky Sports pundit Gary Neville provided scathing on-air commentary during United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last Sunday, before conducting a post-match podcast in the Old Trafford gantry in which he accused some of their players of being unprofessional.

"There's a couple of them... I live in Manchester and they're not that professional, some of them," Neville stated.

"I've got no time for them. There's a few of them that don't go to bed at the right time. Don't eat the right things. Don't think about Manchester United every single minute of every single day."

But it's digital and streaming platforms that are re-defining a new age of analysis.

Neville launched The Overlap in 2021, and its success across video and podcast platforms has seen the channel become one of the most influential outlets in sports media.

On Tuesday, Wayne Rooney appeared on Neville's Manchester United -dedicated YouTube channel 'Stick to United' where he said Carrick's players "need a firework up their a***".

Neville has since hosted his own The Overlap show where he said managers sometimes need to be sacked "for their own good", while ex-United captain Roy Keane said Carrick and his backroom staff are "lucky boys" to still be in jobs.

Neville acquired a network of YouTube channels from United influencer Mark Goldbridge last summer, which has significantly increased the channel's coverage of the club.

Largely known for viral clips of his expletive-laden rants during streamed 'watchalongs' of their matches, Goldbridge's YouTube channels had amassed more than 3.7million subscribers.

Goldbridge - whose real name is Brent di Cesare - now co-hosts the 'Stick to United' show with Rooney, the club's record goalscorer.

But Neville, Rooney and Keane are far from the only ones setting the agenda.

Class of '92 pair Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt co-host their own podcast called 'The Good, The Bad & The Football'.

Before last season's Manchester derby at Old Trafford - Carrick's first home game in charge - Butt said City striker Erling Haaland would "pick Lisandro Martinez up and run with him", while Scholes said the Norway forward would "throw him in the net" after scoring.

United won the game 2-0, with Martinez putting in a stellar performance.

Asked about Scholes' comments after the match, the Argentine defender said: "Honestly, he can say whatever he wants. I told him already, if he wants to say something to me, he can come to wherever he wants. To my house, wherever. I don't care."

Asked during Thursday's news conference how he deals with the 'noise' from former team-mates and ex-players, Carrick said he avoids it as best he can.

"I don't see it really. I see the things that I need to see," he added.

"I don't look for it - it doesn't really help in any way.

"I've said it before, I care about what the supporters think. I care about what it feels like in the stadium, and them travelling to games for us, to come and see us and support us. I care about what we give them, and what we offer them, and what they see. I genuinely don't take any notice of anything else."

How Lineker and Neville became rival media moguls

'Fully committed' Fernandes to remain Man Utd captain

Sometimes managers need sacking for own good - Neville

Where once a low rating in a newspaper could anger players, they now have to deal with days of debate after a bad result or below-par performance.

Former manager Erik ten Hag recently alluded to the difficulty his Manchester United squad had dealing with the opinions of people like Neville and Rio Ferdinand, and said former players could be "more helpful" to the club.

"I did nice interviews with them both [Neville and Ferdinand], so it didn't hurt me. Of course, they have podcasts, they have their models," Ten Hag told The Athletic , external .

"Sometimes it's difficult for players. Some of them get affected by it, get annoyed by it.

"They achieved massive successes. But also, they can help the club more, help the players more. There should be two ways that they support it. But I think always the thing you most love, you most criticise."

Speaking on Ferdinand's podcast , external last summer, it was put to Neville he had been overly critical when covering his boyhood club.

"It's a balance though Rio, isn't it?" he told his former United team-mate.

"It's like, do I want [Manchester] City to win the league? I absolutely don't want City anywhere near the league title."

And he insisted "United are the hardest games I do".

"People might think that I'm more critical of United when they don't play well. Sometimes, over the last maybe 10 years, the balance, maybe I've not got it right," admitted Neville.…

title: How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant
text:
"When I told people what I wanted to do, open shops on the high street selling things for one pound, they said, 'how will you find products to sell for a pound, what about inflation, it will never work.'"

That is how Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, describes the genesis of the budget giant - which went on to employ thousands of people and see over a million customers a week - on his own website , external .

But now the West Midlands-based retailer is teetering on the edge , after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group.

Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators

Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse

The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisis

Having spent time on his parents stall since the age of two Wolverhampton-born businessman Smith started out in the very same place - selling items for £1 from his own stall.

After a £50,000 loan from his parents he opened the first Poundland shop , in The Octagon Shopping Centre in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, on 13 December 1990.

That first day, with a range of 624 products, the store took more than £13,000 - "and Poundland was born," Smith said.

Smith and his wife, Tracy, now based in Shropshire, owned the company for 16 years.

In 2006, he decided the time had come and he sold his final shares in the business for £250m, but later said the sale felt it was "as though somebody had died".

But by 2025, the Walsall-based company was itself sold for just £1 .

Its owner, Polish firm Pepco, confirmed it had sold the brand for a "nominal" sum to US investment firm Gordon Brothers.

At the time Poundland had more than 800 stores across the UK and Ireland and employed around 16,000 staff.

"I did pick up the phone when I heard it was for sale but I was a bit too late," Smith said after the sale.

Now, the retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which will give the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.

A protest was held outside the Poundland HQ on Thursday, Claire Sutcliffe - who has been at the company for nearly a decade - among those demonstrating.

Questioned about how she felt, the 49-year-old replied she was "very sad", adding: "Nine years is a lot working for Poundland and they've been really good to me as a Poundland family, really supportive."

Sutcliffe added that some had worked for the business for 20 years and "it's just very sad for us all".

Asked what her message was to owners Gordon Brothers, she replied: "Please just sell.

"Save our jobs, we've all got families to feed and it's... near Christmas."

Professor Sarah Montano, a retail expert from the University of Birmingham, said: "The real problem for Poundland is, when they first started it was really great because everything was £1, that was a really unique selling point for them.

"[Today] there's competitors which are offering very similar prices and for quite a lot of products they're offering them cheaper."

She added that some competitors had "really got their finger on the key trends".

In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".

"The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs," they said.

"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."

They also thanked "staff, suppliers and customers for their continued support".
